analysis.one_liner: Gives low-income households up to $50 off monthly internet during COVID-19, reimbursing providers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in May 2020 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, it received no further action and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, internet providers would have had to discount low-income households' broadband by up to $50 a month ($75 on Tribal land) — the full advertised rate for many — and could be reimbursed up to $100 for a laptop or tablet. An $8.8 billion federal fund would repay providers, and the FCC's Lifeline program would give enrollees unlimited minutes and data. It also gave states $200 million to link SNAP records to the system that verifies Lifeline eligibility, so food-assistance households would automatically qualify.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households — including families with free or reduced-price school lunch, Lifeline participants, and households with a documented job loss since February 2020 — would get discounted broadband and, for a small copay, a laptop or tablet. Tribal-land households would get a larger discount. The benefit would run through the COVID emergency plus six months, extendable by states or tribes.

how_it_helps.text: Eligible households could get an internet offering discounted by up to $50 a month (up to $75 on Tribal land), with providers repaid from a new $8.8 billion Emergency Broadband Connectivity Fund [S2][S3].

Eligibility would reach beyond existing Lifeline enrollees to households with school-lunch or breakfast benefits or a documented substantial loss of income since February 29, 2020, and eligibility checks would be capped at two days [S3].
Lifeline participants would get unlimited minutes and unlimited 4G data during the emergency, with the program's support amounts increased to cover providers' added cost [S2][S3].
Providers supplying a laptop, desktop, or tablet for a $10-$50 copay could be reimbursed up to $100 per household, helping households without a home computer [S3].
States would get grants to connect SNAP databases to the Lifeline eligibility verifier, so food-assistance receipt would automatically qualify a household for Lifeline [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the $8.8 billion connectivity fund and $200 million in state grants. Providers would be paid the household's full normal advertised rate (as of May 1, 2020) from the fund, so the benefit flows through private companies at full retail price.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes roughly $9 billion in new federal spending, with reimbursements pegged to providers' advertised rates as of May 1, 2020 — including promotional rates — rather than to providers' actual costs, leaving the program's total price open-ended [S3].

The subsidy would run through private broadband providers, who would be paid the normal retail rate from the federal fund, making them the paid middlemen for a public benefit rather than directing money to households [S3].

Providers could choose their own 'alternative verification process' for eligibility instead of the national verifier, though the FCC would have to find it sufficient and providers would face audits and certifications against waste and fraud [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For low-income households locked out of school, work, and telehealth during COVID-19, the benefit was substantial and the design included real safeguards: certification that households are not overcharged, bans on early-termination fees and waiting periods, audit requirements, and FCC enforcement under the Communications Act. The main honest cost is fiscal: nearly $9 billion in new spending, and reimbursements sized to providers' advertised retail prices rather than negotiated bulk rates, which favors the industry. On balance the bill's benefits to households outweigh its costs, though it entrenched providers as the channel for the subsidy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marc Veasey introduced the Emergency Broadband Connections Act of 2020 on May 14, 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never left committee and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].
The bill had one cosponsor, a House Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers came out ahead: they avoided the mandated discounts, unlimited Lifeline service requirements, certifications, audits, and FCC enforcement the bill would have imposed, while the federal government avoided the ~$9 billion cost. Low-income households without affordable internet during the pandemic came out the loser, since the bill died before reaching a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadband providers; low-income households lost out

for.name: Rep. Marc Veasey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 14, 2020, proposing a $50-a-month broadband discount for low-income households during COVID-19, reimbursed from a new $8.8 billion federal fund.

for.name: 1 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: One House Democrat cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 14, 2020, and never reported it out; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had minimal support of any kind — two Democrats in total and no recorded opposition vote — so the record shows no partisan lineup, just inaction.

industries.note: The bill would have made providers the paid channel for a public benefit: they would discount households' bills up to $50 a month and be reimbursed from a $8.8 billion federal fund at each household's normal advertised rate. Because the bill died, providers avoided both the guaranteed revenue stream and the accompanying mandates (unlimited Lifeline service, certifications, audits, and FCC enforcement).

Providers supplying a laptop, desktop, or tablet to eligible households for a $10-$50 copay could claim up to $100 back from the federal fund per household, one device each. With the bill's death, this device subsidy never existed.
States would have received grants (from $200 million) to connect their food-assistance databases to the Lifeline eligibility verifier, easing enrollment checks. The grants were never made.
